paragraphs.text: This [white tea](white:definition) cake comes from [Fuding](fuding:where-it-is), a coastal city in the northeast corner of Fujian, against the Zhejiang border, with mountains on three sides and the East China Sea to the east. Fuding is the place most often named as the [home of white tea](fuding:known-for). Its way of making it, a long natural wither with no frying and no rolling, is listed in China as national cultural heritage.

The cake carries the year 2008, which makes it eighteen years old. The trade has a saying that white tea is tea in its first year, [medicine at three and a treasure at seven](fujian-white:ageing). It is only a saying and has not been tested, and no agreed number of years makes a white tea aged.

[Pressed white tea](fujian-white:cakes) is new. Cakes began in the 2000s and spread around 2010 because a cake is smaller than loose leaf and easier to keep and carry, so this one comes from the style's early years. Some cakes are pressed from leaf that was first aged loose, so the year on a cake can be the year it was pressed rather than the year it was picked.

brewing.text: Gongfu style, use about 1 gram of leaf to 15 to 25 ml of water, for example 5 grams in a 100 to 110 ml gaiwan; weigh it, since the leaf is light and bulky. Silver Needle and young, delicate tea take water below the boil, about 75 to 90°C; older, leafier or aged tea takes water at or near the boil. Start with a steep of 10 to 45 seconds and add a few seconds each round. An aged cake is often rinsed quickly first, and older pressed tea can be simmered on the stove, about 5 grams to 500 ml for 3 to 10 minutes; young, delicate tea is not.

notice.text: Jujube or dried dates, herbs and medicine, wood, honey and dried fruit, a deeper, redder liquor, a thicker, rounder body, and less lift in the scent than a young tea.
